papers.title: Variance Reduction with Delayed Feedback for Non-Convex Optimization
papers.excerpt: We study variance reduction for non-convex optimization when gradient evaluations return with a delay. The server can update the parameter while earlier evaluations remain unfinished. We first analyze an ordered recursive momentum estimator for stochastic optimization. Under average smoothness and bounded variance, its oracle complexity is , where the target is an expected squared gradient norm of at most and bounds the feedback delay. We next study finite sums with components and obtain evaluations. An asynchronous snapshot variant continues updating during full-gradient computations under an explicit bound on their completion time. For the stochastic method, we further replace a maximum-delay bound by a bound on the weighted amount of missing feedback.

papers.title: Primal-Dual Adaptive Subgradient Methods
papers.excerpt: We propose adaptive primal-dual subgradient methods for constrained convex optimization. Our first method applies an AdaGrad-style step-sizes to the dual problem and recovers primal solutions by averaging the associated Fenchel-type oracle outputs. It achieves convergence for the dual objective residual, primal objective residual, and feasibility gap in the nonsmooth regime, while automatically improving to when the dual objective is smooth. We further develop an accelerated variant, which retains the nonsmooth rate while achieving convergence in the smooth regime under mild assumptions. These guarantees require no prior knowledge of the underlying regularity. We demonstrate the empirical performance of the proposed methods on optimal transport and semidefinite relaxation of the Max-Cut problem.

papers.title: Controllability Allocation Scores for Linear Infinite-Dimensional Systems
papers.excerpt: We define finite-time controllability allocation scores (CASs) as optimal solutions to two convex optimization problems that allocate a fixed actuation budget among prescribed input functions of linear infinite-dimensional continuum systems with selected target outputs. The objectives are expressed using controllability Gramians for the selected outputs and correspond to maximizing the volume of output changes reachable with unit control energy or minimizing the mean energy required for unit output changes. To compute these CASs, we discretize the system in space, construct the resulting Gramians, and solve the resulting allocation problems by a domain-aware projected gradient descent method. We study the behavior of CASs when the actuator-to-target responses of the spatially discretized systems converge to those of the continuum system as the mesh is refined.

papers.title: Weak-$L^α$ Noise, Strong Guarantees: Gradient Clipping under Affine Heavy Tails
papers.excerpt: Gradient clipping is a key tool for obtaining high-probability convergence guarantees for stochastic first-order methods under heavy-tailed noise. Existing analyses typically assume a bounded central moment of order , which excludes distributions with tails of order at the critical exponent. In this paper, we consider smooth convex optimization under affine heavy-tailed noise, whose scale may grow with the gradient norm. We derive high-probability convergence guarantees for clipped SGD (Clip-SGD) and its accelerated variant Clip-SSTM under a weak- tail condition, which is strictly weaker than the corresponding moment bound. For , the clipping bounds have the same powers of the clipping level as in the moment case, and both methods attain the additive stochastic rate . The gradient-dependent noise contributes a faster-decaying term of order , up to logarithmic factors. At , we characterize the additional logarithmic factor on the Lorentz scale and establish its necessity for the additive error at fixed confidence.

papers.title: Universal Online Convex Optimization With Delayed Feedback
papers.excerpt: We study universal online convex optimization with delayed feedback. We develop a single algorithm that simultaneously adapts to general convex, strongly convex, and exp-concave losses without prior knowledge of the curvature class or parameters. Our regret bounds match the best known dependence on the time horizon and delays up to doubly logarithmic factors: roughly for convex losses and rates with curved losses, where is the total cumulative delay and is the maximum number of simultaneously missing observations. Our main technical contribution is a delayed meta-learner with a second-order excess-loss guarantee, which enables curvature-adaptive aggregation of delayed base learners. In addition, our new exp-concave base learner yields a sharper regret bound which improves the state-of-the-art delay dependence by replacing the maximum delay with the potentially much smaller , while retaining the complementary dependence.

papers.title: Tight lower bounds for Lipschitz geodesically convex optimization on hyperbolic space
papers.excerpt: We determine the dimension-independent first-order query complexity of minimizing a Lipschitz geodesically convex (g-convex) function on hyperbolic space. Given a ball of radius containing a global minimizer, we prove that queries are necessary to attain accuracy , where is the Lipschitz constant and captures the effect of curvature. This matches the known upper bound for the Riemannian subgradient method (Zhang and Sra, 2016). This is the first query-complexity result for g-convex optimization that is tight simultaneously in curvature and target accuracy. The standard Euclidean recipe of constructing hard instances as maxima of affine functions does not transfer to hyperbolic space, so the lower bound requires a new mechanism. Our starting point is the worst-function construction of Criscitiello and Boumal (2023, Appendix A). It gives the same lower bound for a subclass of algorithms, including the subgradient method, whose queries remain in prescribed g-convex regions.

papers.title: On the Nonoccurrence of Gradient Restart in Nesterov Accelerated Gradient Method
papers.excerpt: Gradient restarting often improves the practical performance of accelerated gradient methods for unconstrained convex optimization problems, but a general theoretical guarantee of such improvement remains unclear. In this paper, we construct smooth, strongly convex objectives with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and corresponding initial points for which gradient restart never occurs, both for Nesterov's accelerated gradient method and for its ordinary differential equation model. From these examples, we conclude that strong convexity and smoothness alone do not guarantee that gradient restart improves the convergence behavior of the accelerated method or its continuous-time model. In particular, for the continuous-time example, the objective gap is asymptotic to . We therefore obtain a negative answer to the open problem raised by Su, Boyd, and Cand{è}s [\textit{J. Mach. Learn. Res.}, 2016, 17(153), 1--43] of whether gradient restart guarantees linear convergence of the continuous dynamics for smooth strongly convex objectives.

papers.title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
papers.excerpt: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions.
